Q: Making SQL queries from a task, not SqlExecuteQueryOperator A:

handle_process.expand(row=rows) returns a MappedOperator whose output property is an XcomArg that can be used to pull in the results of expanded tasks.

Gather the results from this XcomArg in an intermediate task:

mapped_results = handle_row.expand(row=rows)

def format_results_for_grpc_operator(results):
    pass

@task
def prepare_grpc_payload(results: list):
    '''Gather results from fanned out tasks'''
    return format_results_for_grpc_operator(results)

grpc_input = prepare_grpc_payload(mapped_results)

Then push this to the GrpcOperator like so:

submit_task = GrpcOperator(
    task_id='submit_to_grpc',
    data=grpc_input,
)

Q: usefullness of shared_ptr in C interface A:

make_unique can throw std::bad_alloc, and anything that can thrown by the construct of T, which is why it's not noexcept (see cppreference/make_unique). The purpose of std::make_unique is (was, up to C++17, and still is for MSVC to some extent) to provide clear sequence point semantics, and avoid having unexpected reordering between new T and the construction of unique_ptr (Exceptionsafety of make_unique: Why is f(new T) exception safe), it's not to catch everything.

Q: Merging Excels - PowerShell - Import Excel A:

In the case where your worksheet only has a single row, you could use -NoHeader, then what was the actual header becomes the first row and the headers are named as P1 to PX depending on the number columns, this however is definitely not a good solution to the problem.

What I recommend you to use in this case which is a far better and efficient solution is to open them as an ExcelPackage, this way you will avoid the header problem and also should be more efficient considering this probably copies from file stream to file stream without having to hold the hold sheet in memory.

To consider, if the source .xlsx files have more than one worksheet those will be included too in the final.xlsx.

$sourceFolderPath = 'C:\temp\ManipulationTesting\test'
$OutputFilePath = 'C:\temp\ManipulationTesting\test\Final.xlsx'
$i = 0

$finalPkg = Open-ExcelPackage $OutputFilePath -Create
$wsheets = $finalPkg.Workbook.Worksheets

Get-ChildItem $sourceFolderPath -Filter *.xlsx | ForEach-Object {
    $pkg = Open-ExcelPackage $_.FullName
    foreach ($sheet in $pkg.Workbook.Worksheets) {
        $null = $wsheets.Add("Sheet$(($i++))", $sheet)
    }

    $pkg | Close-ExcelPackage
}

$finalPkg | Close-ExcelPackage

Q: How to upgrade systemd to a specific version in ubuntu v18.04? A:

On Ubuntu 18.04, the safest way to get systemd ≥239 is to upgrade to Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, instead of manually updating systemd.

Manual upgrades are only for experienced users with full backups.

No, seriously, full backup.

I AM A EXPERIENCED USER

Oh, you are?

You must have a live USB of Ubuntu ready to repair the system.

Don't go any further than having a live USB of Ubuntu in your hand.

Got the Live Ubuntu USB stick

Backup everything using a full system snapshot (if using LVM or Btrfs):

sudo lvcreate --size 20G --snapshot --name root_snap /dev/ubuntu-vg/root

Or backup important data:

rsync -aAXv /home /etc /var /root /boot /mnt/backup/

Make a bootable Ubuntu USB to recover the system if it fails.

Build dependencies

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git build-essential pkg-config libcap-dev libpam0g-dev libblkid-dev libmount-dev libkmod-dev libselinux1-dev python3-docutils gettext autoconf automake libtool

Download systemd 239 source

wget https://github.com/systemd/systemd/releases/download/v239/systemd-239.tar.gz
tar -xvf systemd-239.tar.gz
cd systemd-239

Configure & compile

./configure --prefix=/usr \
            --sysconfdir=/etc \
            --localstatedir=/var
make -j$(nproc)

WARNING: Check for errors. If any missing libraries are reported, install them first.

Install systemd

sudo make install

This will replace the existing systemd binaries.

WARNING: Do not reboot yet; let’s test first.

Test w/o reboot

sudo systemctl daemon-reexec
systemctl --version

You should see systemd 239.

If it fails, do not reboot. You can restore from the backup or live USB.

Update initranfs & bootload

sudo update-initramfs -u
sudo update-grub

Reboot carefully

Reboot normally:

sudo reboot

If the system fails to boot:

Boot from your Ubuntu live USB.

Mount your root partition:

sudo mount /dev/sdXY /mnt
sudo chroot /mnt

Restore the backup of your original systemd binaries:

rsync -aAXv /backup/usr/lib/systemd/ /usr/lib/systemd/

Update initramfs and reboot.

Verify

systemctl --version

You should see:

systemd 239
+PAM +AUDIT +SELINUX ...

Q: Is the brute-force solution for "Is Binary Tree Balanced" really O(n^2) with early exit? A:

It's true that this algorithm has complexity O(N log N) if the tree is balanced. More precisely it's O(sum of depths of vertices). We need to construct an unbalanced tree that makes it do a lot of work.

The worst case of divide-and-conquer style algorithms like this appears when the two halves are heavily unbalanced - in terms of size, not depth. This distinction allows us to construct something worse than O(N log N), but as it turns out, O(N^2) isn't a tight bound either.

Let's look at the recursion in the top node. An if expr1 and expr2 will evaluate expr1 first.

  • If it was true, the left side is balanced, therefore it has O(log N) depth and since the whole tree's depth must be similar, the total running time will be O(N log N). This clearly isn't our worst case.
  • When it's false, we don't care about how the right side looks since expr2 is never evaluated. It just needs a specific depth. We might as well make it a path with that depth and put all the other vertices (or as many as we need) in the left part.

Let the algorithm recurse to the left K times, finding depths d[0:K+1]. Then the sizes of right subtrees for these recursive steps are at least d[0]-1, ..., d[K-1]-1 and we find that N >= sum(d)+1. The runtime of the algorithm is proportional to the sum of sizes of subtrees in the recursion steps, which is at most N + N-d[0] + ... + N-sum(d[0:K]) = (K+1)N - K d[0] - ... - d[K-1].

From these general formulas and using the fact that d must be a decreasing sequence, we can determine that for any tree, N >= c1 K^2 and runtime <= c2 K N <= c2 N sqrt(N/c1), so the algorithm is O(N sqrt N). At the same time, we've constructed a family of worst case examples leading to this complexity, where all right subtrees are paths to the same depth:

The primary constraint which makes this algorithm subquadratic is that depths found in subsequent recursion steps are highly dependent on each other; that it's checking if the tree is balanced is almost irrelevant since "the left-right depths differ by at most 1" has no implication on balancedness if it's only true a few times. However, this constraint isn't strong enough to forbid highly unbalanced trees.

Q: How to best prepare an offline database app for future synchronization with an online server A:

Room isn't a database. It's a library for generating SQL querries. The db used in Android is SQLite. And really my suggestion would be- don't use SQLite. There are dbs like firebase, couchbase, etc which have the syncing functionality built in. Use one of them. Because writing the syncing functionality can be a true nightmare if you need full bidirectional sync. Ever heard the old joke that "the only hard problems in CS are cache coherency and naming things"? Syncing is literally cache coherency, one of the hardest things to do right.
